value.overview: The Lesser Black-backed Gull is a large, long-winged gull that breeds mainly in northern Europe and western Russia. It is smaller and slimmer than the Great Black-backed Gull and usually has yellow legs, a dark gray to black back, and black wingtips. Adults have a yellow bill with a red spot. Outside the breeding season, it uses a wide range of coastal and inland waters and often gathers with other gulls.
value.classification: The Lesser Black-backed Gull belongs to the gull family Laridae and the order Charadriiformes. Its scientific name is Larus fuscus.
value.identification: Adults have white underparts, a dark slate-gray to black back, black wingtips with limited white markings, yellow legs, and a yellow bill with a red spot on the lower mandible. The head is usually white in breeding plumage but becomes brown-streaked in winter. It has long, pointed wings and a relatively slender shape. Juveniles are brown and heavily mottled, gradually acquiring adult plumage over about four years.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds across northern and western Europe, the Baltic region, Iceland, and parts of northern and western Russia. During migration and winter it occurs around the North Atlantic, Mediterranean, western Africa, and parts of the Americas. In Costa Rica it is an accidental, very uncommon visitor rather than a resident or breeding species. Reliable records are associated with coastal areas and offshore waters, where it may appear among mixed gull flocks, especially during dispersal or migration.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Most populations move south after breeding, while some remain near breeding areas. In Costa Rica it is classified as accidental, with only occasional records and no known regular seasonal presence.
value.breeding: Breeding usually occurs in colonies on coastal islands, cliffs, dunes, saltmarshes, and sometimes islands in lakes or rivers. The nest is a shallow structure made from grasses and other vegetation, placed on the ground. A typical clutch contains two or three eggs. Both adults incubate the eggs and feed the chicks, which are protected within the colony and become independent after fledging.
value.dietFeeding: The Lesser Black-backed Gull is an opportunistic omnivore. It eats fish, marine invertebrates, crustaceans, mollusks, insects, worms, carrion, eggs, small birds, rodents, berries, seeds, and discarded food. It forages by walking, swimming, diving shallowly, or catching prey at the surface. It also scavenges around fishing vessels, harbors, landfills, farmland, and other places where food is concentrated.
value.behavior: This gull is often social outside the breeding season and commonly rests or feeds in mixed-species flocks. It is an adaptable and strong-flying bird that can travel long distances between feeding and roosting sites. Individuals may follow fishing boats, patrol beaches, search tidal zones, or forage inland. Adults defend nesting territories, while nonbreeding birds may gather in resting groups near breeding colonies or productive feeding areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered stable to increasing, although trends differ among regions and some local populations have declined.
